paras: The lynching of Andrew Diggs was the hanging of a Black man by a masked mob at Scottsboro, Jackson County, Alabama, on the night of June 29–30, 1903, after the mob shot down Sheriff D. O. Austin and took Diggs from the county jail. Diggs had been jailed the day before, accused of attempting to assault the daughter of a Larkinsville physician. Five young white men were arrested, but the county grand jury found no evidence to indict, and Alabama papers treated the case as the state's only lynching of 1903.

Diggs, called "Andy Diggs" by the Montgomery Advertiser, was arrested on Sunday evening, charged with attempting a criminal assault on Miss Alma Smith, 19, daughter of Dr. B. B. Smith of Larkinsville. The Associated Press dispatch added that he "made a confession to the brother of the young lady and others who visited the jail," a claim attributed to no named witness.

Between midnight and daybreak about seventy-five masked men entered the downstairs hall of the jail. Austin seized two pistols, climbed to the cells and warned that he would kill anyone who came up; the mob answered with a volley, and he emptied his revolver before he was shot in the right leg and his pistol arm. His daughter, named in the Advertiser as Miss Ola Austin, was held at pistol point until she surrendered the keys, while the jail's telephone wires had been cut.

Diggs was led out with a halter to the west end of town and hanged from the arm of a telegraph pole. His body was "being viewed by hundreds of people" the next morning, was cut down about noon on June 30, and was given to his father, Mose Diggs, for burial at Larkinsville.

Governor Jelks praised the sheriff, asked Judge J. A. Bilbro to call a special term of court, and directed Solicitor Proctor to investigate. On July 1 a deputy arrested five Larkinsville men, Walker McCutchen, Ed Harris, Albert Smith, Roy Kelly and Bob Brannan, whom the Age-Herald called "of the most prominent families in Jackson county"; the Providence News identified Smith as the girl's brother.

At a hearing on July 3 four were bound over on $2,000 bail each and McCutcheon was discharged on proof that he had been sick at home. During their detention, the Advertiser noted, they received "many flowers and delicacies." Bilbro, at the request of county officials, declined to call an extra term, leaving the case for the regular term opening August 31.

In September the grand jury reported that it had "failed to secure evidence sufficient to justify indictments against the offenders of the law." No report of an inquest or a trial appears in the coverage.

The AP story ran on June 30 in the Washington Evening Star under "ANOTHER NEGRO LYNCHED" and the next day in the Wichita Daily Eagle, both repeating the confession claim. In Alabama the Montgomery Advertiser centered the "BRAVE SHERIFF SHOT BY MOB OF LYNCHERS" and his daughter. The Birmingham Age-Herald called the lynching "wholly uncalled for on any ground save that of passion" while treating Diggs's guilt as settled, and its Huntsville column called him "a negro rapist." In October it wrote that justice would not be done unless a jury punished the men who shot the sheriff.

The Wisconsin Weekly Advocate ran the dispatch on July 2 under "SHERIFF IS SHOT PROTECTING NEGRO," and the Savannah Tribune gave the fullest Black-press account on July 4 as a "Sensational Lynching," printing the name "Dlimms." The Baltimore Afro-American's digest named him "Albert Diggs" and stated that he "had assaulted a white woman." The Indianapolis Freeman listed Diggs among June's lynchings, and monthly lists in both presses dated the killing June 29, June 30 or July 1.

The Advertiser's correspondent and the Savannah Tribune placed the hanging at a telegraph pole in town, while a wire version printed in Wichita said Diggs was "taken to the woods and hanged"; the local report is the more direct. The first reports also have the sheriff's daughter forced at gunpoint to give up the keys, while the Advertiser's next-day letter says she "with pistols in hand defied the mob."

reader.title: Lynching of Andrew Diggs
bases: A masked mob took Diggs, held on an assault charge, from the Scottsboro jail after shooting the sheriff and hanged him from a telegraph pole (A4, A1, A17).

Every full report says Diggs was hanged by a mob of masked men, about seventy-five by the local account, who shot the sheriff to get him (A1, A4, A17); he was held on an accusation of attempted assault on a white girl, and five men were later arrested for murder (A12, A16).

The AP wire (A1), the Montgomery Advertiser's own Scottsboro correspondent (A4, A13), Birmingham Age-Herald reports (A14, A16) and the grand jury report (A41) agree on the hanging, the shooting of the sheriff and the arrests.

framing.detail: The Evening Star ran the AP story under 'ANOTHER NEGRO LYNCHED' with the subhead 'Attempted Criminal Assault on Prominent Young Lady', repeating the confession claim.
The Montgomery Advertiser headlined the 'BRAVE SHERIFF' and praised him and his daughter, called the arrested men 'young men of Larkinsville', and noted the flowers and delicacies they received.

The Birmingham Age-Herald editorially called the lynching 'wholly uncalled for' and urged punishment of the ringleaders, yet treated Diggs's guilt as established and elsewhere called him 'a negro rapist'.

The Wisconsin Weekly Advocate, Savannah Tribune and Rising Son reprinted white wire or syndicated text, including the confession claim, under headings such as 'SHERIFF IS SHOT PROTECTING NEGRO' and 'Sensational Lynching'.
The Indianapolis Freeman counted Diggs in its roll of June lynchings and in its local column hoped June 'will never again be so big with difficulties'.
